Generative AI with LLM

MITB CS614 · August Term 2026

This course traces the path from turning text into vectors to adapting large language models efficiently. Classes run on Tuesdays, 7:00pm-10:15pm, from 25 August to 3 November 2026.

Course at a glance

Assessment Weight What it covers
Seven in-class quizzes 49% Seven quizzes, each worth 7%; they test preceding course content.
Course feedback 1% End-of-course feedback submission.
Group project 40% A 2-5 person LLM system or applied study, with report, presentation, and code. Due Tuesday, 3 November 2026.
Participation 10% Attendance, engagement, and weekly reflections.

Study chapters

Chapter Topic Focus
Chapter 1: Text processing & embeddings Text Processing Fundamentals Tokens, n-grams, BOW, TF-IDF, cosine similarity, and Word2Vec.
Chapter 2: Transformers & LLMs Transformers Attention, transformer blocks, BERT, and multimodal models.
Chapter 3: Training & customising LLMs Training Pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, cross-entropy, training curves, and alignment.
Chapter 4: Efficient fine-tuning Customising LLMs The customisation ladder, LoRA/QLoRA, precision, and efficient training.

AI-use rules

AI tools are part of the subject, but their use depends on the setting.

Setting AI use
Class discussion and quizzes Not allowed. These activities show your own reasoning and understanding.
Group-project code, system, and study work Allowed.
Written report Allowed as assistance only. The responsible student must edit and verify every claim, citation, number, and code snippet.
Final presentation Not allowed. Each student explains their contribution without an LLM-generated script, phone, notes, or slides as a script.

Final group project

Choose a real or domain-specific problem and build a working GenAI system or a rigorous applied study. Arrange a scope-and-task-distribution meeting for approval once the team has an idea.

A strong project is technically correct, reproducible, evaluated both quantitatively and qualitatively, and compares at least two meaningful alternatives. The report should explain the motivation, architecture, data and model choices, experimental method, results, trade-offs, risks, and future work. Include reproducible artefacts such as a repository, README, configuration, and fixed seeds where appropriate.

Possible directions include a domain RAG assistant with an advanced retrieval method, a fine-tuned tutor evaluated against its base model, a multi-agent analysis workflow, or a study comparing RAG, fine-tuning, robustness, or agent-memory strategies.

How the four chapters connect

Chapter 1 makes text measurable. Chapter 2 explains the architecture that makes those representations context-aware. Chapter 3 shows how the architecture learns, and Chapter 4 focuses on deciding whether fine-tuning is warranted and how to do it within practical hardware limits. Later course sessions extend this foundation to inference, evaluation, RAG, agents, advanced architectures, and responsible use.
